text.content:
Six items, one for each Crow, that grow as their bearers do. They are not treasure and they are not upgrades — none of them makes an attack land harder or a spell save higher. Each one makes a particular way of playing steadily more powerful.

The Four States

StateRarityLevelsChargesRecovery
DormantUncommon3–53all of them
AwakenedRare6–95all of them
ExaltedVery Rare10–1471d6 + 1
LegendaryLegendary15+91d8 + 1

A bigger pool refills more slowly. That is deliberate: at Exalted and Legendary the question stops being can I afford this and becomes is this the day I spend it.

A legacy item keeps every feature from its earlier states unless a later feature explicitly replaces one. Where that happens, the older version simply stops being offered.

Legacy Save DC

8 + proficiency bonus + the bearer's primary ability modifier.

For Alice, Solanthis, Jinx and Sylas that is their spellcasting ability; the items are configured to read it from the character sheet, so it follows a class change without editing. For Clipper it is Wisdom and for Kattal it is Strength, both set explicitly.

What Foundry Does On Its Own

These are ordinary dnd5e items, not macros, and almost all of the bookkeeping is automatic once one is on a character sheet:

  • Features appear when they are earned. Every feature is an activity carrying a minimum character level. Below that level it is not on the sheet at all, so a player never has to remember which half of the item they are allowed to use.
  • Superseded features vanish. Solanthis' first Not Them disappears the moment the Awakened version arrives; the same for Jinx's spell-bending and Contingency.
  • The charge pool resizes itself at levels 6, 10 and 15.
  • Recovery changes with it. Dormant and Awakened refill completely at dawn; Exalted and Legendary roll for it. The Shepherd's Lantern does all of this at dusk instead.
  • Charges are spent by using the feature, and features limited per rest track their own uses.

The Two Things You Do By Hand

  • Clipper's Sure Footing. A climbing speed cannot gate itself on level the way a charge pool can, so it ships as a switched-off effect on the item. Turn it on in the Effects tab when the Knot awakens.
  • Sylas' Not Yet. It recharges after seven days, which is not a rest, so it has no automatic recovery at all. Once he has actually brought someone back, clear the use by hand a week later.

Everything else, including Kattal's carrying capacity, gates itself.

Handing Them Out

The items live in the Wayreth — Crow Legacy Items compendium rather than loose in the Item Directory, because each one is bound to a named character. Drag one onto its bearer's sheet, and have them attune.

A bearer at 3rd level sees three or four things they can do. The rest of the text is visible in the item description, which is worth leaving readable: knowing the shape of what is coming is most of the pleasure, and none of it is usable early.

The Player Reference Sheets

Each item also has its own journal — Alice — The Crown of Little Wonders, Kattal — Ispin's Unmoving Nail and so on — written for the player who carries it. Each one has a quick-reference page with the charge table and a level-by-level list of what unlocks when, a page per state, and a page of play tips and the rulings most likely to come up.

They install visible to the whole party, because the module cannot know which of your players is which Crow. If you would rather each player saw only their own, open each journal's ownership and set the one player to Observer and Default to None. Nothing else changes if you do.

These journals are generated from the same source as the items themselves, so they cannot drift: if you edit an item's rules, rebuild and the reference sheet follows. If you edit one by hand instead, it will be refreshed on the next module update like any other managed page.

If you would rather keep a later state secret, the items carry the unidentified name Unidentified Legacy Relic — untick Identified and the description is hidden until you restore it.

The level band says when an item may advance. The trigger says when it has earned it. Both should be true.

Every trigger below is a choice rather than an achievement. None of them can be completed by winning a fight, and none of them can be planned for by the player in advance — which is the point. When a Crow does the thing, the item answers that night.

Alice — The Crown of Little Wonders

  • Awakened. She openly acknowledges something genuinely important to her rather than hiding it behind humour, bravado or performance, and then acts on it.
  • Exalted. She deliberately risks something she values because another person's happiness, safety or sense of wonder matters more to her than avoiding hurt herself.
  • Legendary. She willingly chooses genuine belonging, knowing that loving people gives the world something it can take from her.

Solanthis — Ispin's Promise

  • Awakened. He has the means to force someone onto what he believes is the correct course, and deliberately lets them decide for themselves.
  • Exalted. He accepts a serious personal risk because his preparation can protect others, with a safer option available to him.
  • Legendary. Imposing his will would be easier and possibly safer, and he finds a way to protect people without taking their agency from them.

Jinx — The Coin That Lands Sideways

  • Awakened. He has a real chance to escape serious danger and deliberately stays because something or someone matters more.
  • Exalted. He knowingly takes a dangerous magical risk for something more important than proving he can.
  • Legendary. Chance, magic and bravado could hand him extraordinary personal power, and he gambles it for somebody else.

Sylas — The Shepherd's Lantern

  • Awakened. He knowingly accepts a meaningful personal consequence in exchange for knowledge capable of protecting another person.
  • Exalted. Something fundamentally challenges his understanding of death or cosmic order, and he chooses understanding over denial without surrendering his principles.
  • Legendary. He is offered the chance to violate the boundary of death for something he desperately wants, and consciously defines where his line lies.

Clipper — The Wayfarer's Knot

  • Awakened. He gives up progress toward an important objective to go back for someone or something that would otherwise be left behind.
  • Exalted. He guides others through a journey he personally has compelling reason not to return from.
  • Legendary. He must choose between completing an extraordinary journey and returning for someone who needs him, and returns, knowing the chance may never come again.

Kattal — Ispin's Unmoving Nail

  • Awakened. He holds something dangerous back, or supports something failing, when letting go would be safer for him.
  • Exalted. He deliberately makes himself the barrier between overwhelming danger and creatures who cannot withstand it.
  • Legendary. He stands against something he cannot reasonably overpower because someone behind him needs him to remain standing.

Ispin's Two

Two of the six were Ispin Greenshield's own: the brass compass and the black iron spike. He gave them away rather than leaving them, and he explained neither. If the party ever asks why a Solamnic squire's belongings were worth keeping, the honest answer is that he kept coming back for people, and the objects learned it from him.

Six mechanical identities, deliberately non-overlapping. If two of these ever feel interchangeable at the table, something has drifted.

CrowItemIdentityThe sentence it produces
AliceThe Crown of Little WondersCreative problem-solving"What if I try this?"
SolanthisIspin's PromisePreparation and protection"I thought this might happen."
JinxThe Coin That Lands SidewaysPush-your-luck magic"Okay, but what if I gamble again?"
SylasThe Shepherd's LanternKnowledge at a price"I need to understand it."
ClipperThe Wayfarer's KnotNavigation and rescue"I'm going back for them."
KattalIspin's Unmoving NailPhysical protection"Get behind me."

Balance Notes

None of these needs a +1/+2/+3 progression. Class progression already makes their attacks and spells better; the legacies are there so that the thing each player already enjoys doing keeps getting more possible.

Three places to watch:

  • Jinx's psychic bills are real. Push Your Luck and All In each ship a separate damage activity so the cost lands visibly in chat. If he stops taking the damage, the feature stops being a gamble.
  • Sylas pays in hit points and Hit Dice, not charges, for his best information. Forbidden Inquiry and Let Me Understand consume Hit Dice directly, and those Hit Dice stay spent.
  • Kattal's Last Wall costs him his movement. Resistance to all damage is a lot; a speed of 0 for a minute is what pays for it. Do not let him forget the second half.

Interactions Worth Knowing

  • Alice's Follow the Kender is a rider on Rabbit Hole, so it costs 1 charge on top of the 2 the teleport already costs.
  • Solanthis' The Promise and No One Gets Left Behind both require concentration, so he cannot run both, and neither survives a concentration spell.
  • Jinx's All In replaces the normal Double or Nothing spend — 2 charges instead of 1, not in addition to it.
  • Sylas' Hold the Door and Alice's Happily Ever After both catch a creature at 0 hit points. If both trigger on the same creature, the first one resolves and the second is not needed; let the player who declared first spend.
  • Kattal's Living Rampart can redirect an attack onto himself, which stacks badly with The Last Wall in his favour — resistance to all damage plus attacks being aimed at him is the intended pay-off of that combination, and it costs both a long-rest use and his mobility.
